claims.claim: President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act into law on June 29, 1956.
claims.episode_span: In June 1956, President Dwight Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act
claims.supporting_quote: was enacted on June 29, 1956, when President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the bill into law.

claims.claim: The 1956 Act authorized construction of 41,000 miles of the Interstate Highway System.
claims.supporting_quote: for the construction of 41,000 miles (66,000 km) of the Interstate Highway System over a 10-year period, it was the largest public works project in American history through that time.

claims.claim: The Highway Trust Fund paid 90 percent of interstate construction costs, with states paying the remaining 10 percent.
claims.episode_span: The legislation offered 90 percent federal funding
claims.supporting_quote: The money for the Interstate Highway and Defense Highways was handled in a Highway Trust Fund that paid for 90 percent of highway construction costs with the states required to pay the remaining 10 percent.

claims.claim: Eisenhower credited his observation of the German Autobahn network during World War II with convincing him of the value of modern highways.
claims.episode_span: Eisenhower had seen the value of Germany’s autobahns during World War II and returned convinced
claims.supporting_quote: That experience on the Lincoln Highway, plus his observations of the German Autobahn network during World War II , may have convinced him to support construction of the Interstate System when he became president. "The old convoy had started me thinking about good, two-lane highways, but Germany had made me see the wisdom of broader ribbons across the land."

claims.claim: The Cross Bronx Expressway was conceived by Robert Moses and its construction required relocating as many as 60,000 residents.
claims.episode_span: Robert Moses routed the Cross Bronx Expressway through the Tremont and East Tremont sections
claims.supporting_quote: The Cross Bronx Expressway is blamed for worsening the decay of neighborhoods in the South Bronx and required relocating as many as 60,000 residents.

claims.claim: Robert Caro's account holds that Moses deliberately directed the Cross Bronx through East Tremont despite a viable alternative route one block south.
claims.episode_span: rather than through parkland farther north, citing lower property-acquisition costs
claims.supporting_quote: The writer Robert Caro , in his book The Power Broker , argues that Moses intentionally directed the expressway through this neighborhood, even though there was a more viable option only one block south.

claims.claim: Detroit's Black Bottom and Paradise Valley neighborhoods were demolished for slum clearance and freeway construction (I-375 / the Chrysler Freeway).
claims.episode_span: Detroit’s planners aligned I-75 and I-375 through Black Bottom and Paradise Valley
claims.supporting_quote: In the early 1960s, the Black Bottom and Paradise Valley neighborhoods were demolished for the purpose of slum clearance and to make way for the construction of I-375 highway .

claims.claim: San Francisco's Embarcadero Freeway was demolished after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake.
claims.episode_span: San Francisco removed the Embarcadero Freeway after the 1989 earthquake
claims.supporting_quote: The Embarcadero Freeway, which had only been constructed from Broadway along the Embarcadero to the Bay Bridge, was demolished after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake ,

claims.claim: Milwaukee's Park East Freeway was demolished in the early 2000s and the corridor redeveloped.
claims.episode_span: Milwaukee dismantled a mile of the Park East Freeway in 2003, returning the land to taxable development
claims.supporting_quote: The only built portion was demolished beginning in 2002, most of which was replaced by an improved at-grade West McKinley Avenue and East Knapp Street and a new vertical-lift bridge over the Milwaukee River .
